title: Panthers' RT Moton Coughs Up Blood, Reveals Hidden Blood Clot – ESPN Report
body:
Carolina Panthers offensive tackle Taylor Moton revealed Tuesday that a frightening bout of coughing up blood in late June led to the discovery of multiple blood clots, an ailment that forced him to miss the entire training camp and the first two months of the regular season. The 32‑year‑old veteran, who has started every game at right tackle for the Panthers since being drafted in 2017, said the symptoms prompted an immediate medical evaluation that uncovered a serious clotting issue, sidelining him until early November.

Moton’s disclosure shines a light on a health concern that, while relatively rare among NFL players, can have life‑threatening consequences if left untreated. Blood clots form when blood thickens and aggregates, potentially traveling to the lungs, brain, or heart. In the high‑impact environment of professional football, injuries that damage blood vessels or cause prolonged immobility can increase risk, prompting teams to maintain vigilant screening protocols. The Panthers’ medical staff acted swiftly, ordering imaging studies after Moton reported the blood‑tinged cough, and subsequently placed him on the injured reserve list while they administered anticoagulant therapy.

The timing of the diagnosis proved especially costly for the Panthers, who entered the 2024 season with a revamped offensive line after a series of free‑agent moves and draft acquisitions. Moton’s absence forced the coaching staff to reshuffle the line, inserting younger players and shifting veterans to new positions. While the unit managed to stay competitive, the lack of a seasoned anchor at right tackle contributed to inconsistencies in pass protection and run blocking, particularly against power‑run schemes that exploit the edges. Analysts note that the Panthers’ offensive efficiency dropped in the first eight games, a trend that coincided with Moton’s unavailability.

Beyond the on‑field impact, Moton’s experience underscores the broader conversation about player health and the hidden dangers of clotting disorders. Recent years have seen an uptick in reported cases of deep‑vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism among athletes across sports, prompting the NFL to enhance its medical guidelines. The league now mandates routine blood‑coagulation screenings for players who experience unexplained shortness of breath, leg swelling, or, as in Moton’s case, hemoptysis. Moreover, teams are encouraged to educate players on early warning signs and to prioritize rest and mobility after injuries that could predispose them to clot formation.

Moton’s personal reaction was one of relief mixed with frustration. He expressed gratitude for the prompt medical attention that likely averted a more serious outcome, but also lamented the lost time with his teammates and the disruption to his conditioning routine. “I never imagined I’d be dealing with something like this in the middle of a season,” he told reporters. “The doctors were amazing, and I’m just focused on getting back to full strength and helping the team win.” His optimism is bolstered by the fact that, after a month of anticoagulant treatment and close monitoring, follow‑up scans indicated the clots have resolved and no residual blockage remains.

Looking ahead, the Panthers will aim to reintegrate Moton into the lineup as soon as his clearance is confirmed, likely in the latter half of the season when the team’s playoff push intensifies. His return could stabilize the offensive line, offering veteran leadership and improved protection for quarterback Bryce Davis. Meanwhile, the franchise’s medical department plans to review its screening protocols to catch similar issues earlier, potentially instituting periodic blood‑work checks during the preseason. As the Panthers navigate the remainder of the schedule, Moton’s health saga serves as a reminder that player safety extends beyond concussions and musculoskeletal injuries, encompassing the full spectrum of medical challenges that can arise in the demanding world of professional football.
